studies.title: Halving violence against children by treating the parents' own distress
studies.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: a large, prospectively registered, pragmatic RCT with unusually big effect sizes in a setting where trials are rare; limited by self-reported violence measures.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers randomized 479 migrant and displaced caregivers from Myanmar living in Thailand to "Parenting for Resilience" — a co-designed program delivered by non-specialists that tackles caregiver mental health and parenting skills at the same time — or to information about local services. Six months after the program ended, physical violence against children in the intervention group had fallen by roughly half (IRR 0.48) and psychological violence by nearly a third, while caregivers' psychological distress, post-traumatic stress symptoms, emotion regulation and psychological flexibility all improved.
studies.why_it_matters: Most parenting programs treat parenting as a skills-deficit problem; this trial suggests that helping caregivers regulate their own emotions may be the lever that shifts how they treat their children — and that lay workers can deliver it in a displacement camp setting.
studies.pitch_angle: The intervention did not primarily teach discipline techniques — it taught distressed adults how to handle their own feelings, and violence against their children dropped by half. Open on a caregiver in Mae Sot attending a group session run by a neighbor, not a psychologist. Call Amanda Sim (McMaster) or Eve Puffer (Duke). Note the notable null: children's own emotional and behavioral difficulties did not change over the trial window.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a global development or humanitarian outlet on the "task-shifting" revolution — mental health care delivered by trained non-specialists in refugee and conflict settings, and whether donors will fund something that looks like therapy rather than food and shelter.
studies.caveats: Violence and distress outcomes are caregiver self-reported, which risks social desirability bias in an unblinded trial; control condition was information only, not an active comparator; six-month follow-up; findings may not generalize beyond displaced Myanmar communities.

studies.title: It's how impulsive you feel today, not how impulsive you are, that predicts suicidal thoughts
studies.ns_score_reason: 30 days of intensive real-time data overturning a trait-based view of suicide risk; held back by a modest, self-selected sample.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A community sample of 103 adults with recent, repeated suicidal ideation (mean age 33) completed a baseline assessment and then 30 days of ecological momentary assessment, reporting stressful events, impulsivity, emotion dysregulation and suicidal thoughts as they went about their lives. Daily stressors were linked to suicidal ideation only when a person's impulsivity was higher than their own personal average at that moment; stable trait impulsivity showed no such interaction. Emotion dysregulation predicted ideation both as a trait and, more strongly, as a momentary state.
studies.why_it_matters: Clinical risk assessment leans heavily on stable personality traits, but this suggests the dangerous window opens when someone's usual self-control temporarily dips — which is exactly the kind of signal a phone could in principle detect.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the deviation-from-your-own-baseline idea: the risky moment isn't when an impulsive person hits a bad day, it's when anyone becomes more impulsive than they normally are. Open on the mechanics of an EMA study — a phone buzzing six times a day for a month. Call Anne Knorr or Brooke Ammerman, and press them on what a "just-in-time" intervention would actually do when triggered.
studies.wider_angle: A specialist digital health or technology feature on whether passive smartphone sensing can ethically flag suicide risk in real time — covering false positives, consent, and what happens to the data.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation); N=103 with high proportions of gender and sexual minority participants, which may limit generalization; all outcomes self-reported; only concurrent, not prospective, ideation showed the key interaction.

studies.title: Feeling seen as human by political opponents softens partisan hostility — and disgust is the reason
studies.ns_score_reason: five studies across three countries and a surprising emotional pathway; mostly correlational and attitudinal rather than behavioral.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Across five studies with 1,541 participants in the UK, US and Canada, researchers measured "meta-humanization" — the belief that the other political side sees your group as fully human — and tested anger, disgust and empathy as parallel routes to conciliatory attitudes. Meta-humanization consistently predicted less affective polarization and more willingness to negotiate, cooperate and meet the other side, and the dominant emotional pathway was reduced disgust, not increased empathy. Perceived threat to social cohesion moderated the effect, driving it most strongly at moderate levels.
studies.why_it_matters: Depolarization efforts usually try to build empathy; this points instead at a more visceral emotion — moral disgust — as the thing that has to be downregulated before people will talk to each other.
studies.pitch_angle: Empathy may be the wrong target. Open on the experience of discovering that your political opponents don't actually think you're subhuman — and what that does to the gut-level revulsion that keeps partisans apart. Call Melissa Pavetich (Heriot-Watt Dubai) or Sofia Stathi (Greenwich), and ask whether meta-humanization can be manipulated at scale or only measured.
studies.wider_angle: A politics-and-media piece for a current affairs outlet on the incentive structure that keeps each side convinced the other has written them off as inhuman — and what platforms and campaign strategists gain from it.
studies.caveats: Largely cross-sectional and correlational; outcomes are self-reported attitudes and intentions rather than actual contact behavior; Anglophone Western samples only.

studies.title: Resilience stops teenage distress starting — but won't get you out of it
studies.ns_score_reason: a very large prospective cohort with a genuinely asymmetric result; weakened by the fact that everything is self-reported and one-year follow-up.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 9,035 Chinese children and adolescents aged 10 to 17 across two waves 12 months apart, measuring gut symptoms (Rome IV criteria), depression, anxiety, suicidal behavior and resilience. Four profiles emerged, from healthy (~60%) to severe somatic-emotional distress (~6%), and they were sticky: 81% of healthy teens stayed healthy and 56% of severely distressed teens stayed severe. Higher baseline resilience — especially emotion regulation, family support and interpersonal help-seeking — substantially reduced the odds of sliding into distress, but did not predict recovery for anyone already in the mild or severe groups.
studies.why_it_matters: "Resilience training" is sold as a universal fix, but here it behaves like a preventive measure only — once a teenager's body and mood are both affected, personal resilience does nothing to pull them out.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the asymmetry — resilience as a fence at the top of the cliff, not an ambulance at the bottom. Open on the roughly 6% of teenagers whose stomach pain, anxiety and low mood cluster together and barely budge over a year. Call Yun Tao (Yunnan Normal University). Careful framing: this is observational, so avoid implying resilience programs are proven to prevent anything.
studies.wider_angle: A health feature on the gut–brain relationship in adolescence for a general-interest outlet — why functional gastrointestinal disorders, anxiety and self-harm risk travel together, and how often teenagers with recurrent abdominal pain are never asked about their mood.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot establish causation); entirely self-report, including gut symptom diagnosis; two waves only, so transition estimates are coarse; single-country sample.

studies.title: Transcendental meditation cuts workplace stress in a six-month randomized trial
studies.ns_score_reason: a proper randomized trial with six months of follow-up on a much-hyped technique; open-label with no active comparator, so expectancy effects are wide open.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Australian university staff were randomized to Transcendental Meditation training (five days plus regular practice, n=65) or to usual workplace wellbeing resources (n=64), and assessed at baseline, three and six months. The TM group showed a moderate reduction in perceived stress (adjusted mean difference −2.25; Hedges' g = −0.52), plus improvements in anxiety, depression, burnout, sleep quality, wellbeing and health-related quality of life. Exploratory analysis found the twice-daily practitioners accounted for most of the gains.
studies.why_it_matters: Workplace wellbeing programs have a poor evidence record — a recent large UK analysis found most do nothing — so a six-month randomized result with a moderate effect size is worth examining closely, including its weaknesses.
studies.pitch_angle: Against a backdrop of evidence that corporate mindfulness apps and resilience workshops mostly fail, one technique held up for six months. Open on an academic doing 20 minutes at their desk twice a day. Call Barbora de Courten (RMIT) — and ask hard about the missing active comparator, since sitting quietly twice a day may be the whole story. Flag that the dose-response finding is exploratory.
studies.wider_angle: A business or work-culture piece for a specialist outlet on why employers keep buying wellbeing products that don't work, and what a genuinely evidence-graded procurement standard for workplace mental health would look like.
studies.caveats: Open-label with no active control or blinding; all primary outcomes self-reported; single institution; N=129; dose-response analysis exploratory; TM is delivered by a commercial organization, though no industry funding is declared.

studies.title: AI-written stories only calm you down if they are both coherent and about you
studies.ns_score_reason: a neat, registered component-dismantling experiment with a striking backfire effect; small N and a single session.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Eighty-seven participants were randomized to read AI-generated text in one of three forms: a coherent narrative about their own situation, a coherent narrative that wasn't personalized, or personalized content with no narrative structure. Only the complete version — coherent *and* personalized — reduced state anxiety and lifted positive affect. The personalized-but-fragmented version actually made positive affect worse.
studies.why_it_matters: "Writing it out" is one of the most commonly recommended emotion regulation tools; this is the first experiment to separate its ingredients, and it suggests that surfacing personal material without organizing it into a story can leave people worse off.
studies.pitch_angle: Journaling advice, tested to destruction — and a warning about the half-done version. Open on the AI-generated text itself: a chatbot handed your worries back to you either as a story or as a jumble. Call Bo Wang (Jiangsu Normal University). This also lands squarely in the current debate about chatbots as emotional support, since the manipulation was literally an LLM.
studies.wider_angle: A technology feature on AI mental health tools for a tech-focused outlet: if narrative structure is the active ingredient, chatbots that merely reflect your feelings back at you may be running the condition that backfired.
studies.caveats: Small N (87); single laboratory session with immediate outcomes only; state anxiety and affect self-reported; no follow-up; findings from a Chinese student-age sample.

studies.title: Teenagers' emotional habits track their own reading of the family, not their parents'
studies.ns_score_reason: a big dyadic dataset with a clean division of labor between closeness and conflict; cross-sectional, so causal direction is unresolved.
studies.the_study: Using 1,875 Chinese parent–adolescent dyads (adolescents mean age 13; 76.5% of parents were mothers), researchers used polynomial regression and response surface analysis to test what happens when parent and child agree or disagree about how close and how conflictual their relationship is. Agreed-upon closeness went with more cognitive reappraisal; agreed-upon conflict went with less reappraisal and more expressive suppression. Crucially, teenagers who saw less closeness or more conflict than their parents did reported the worst emotion regulation profile — and the adolescent's own perception mattered more than the parent's throughout, consistently across early, middle and late adolescence.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the mismatch itself — a parent who thinks things are fine while their teenager doesn't — is where the emotional cost sits, and that closeness and conflict shape different regulation strategies rather than being two ends of one scale.
studies.pitch_angle: The parents in this study who believed the relationship was warmer than their child did had teenagers who bottled things up. Open on that mismatch. Call Yanfang Li (Beijing Normal University), and ask whether the discrepancy is cause, consequence, or both.
studies.wider_angle: A parenting-science piece for a general-interest outlet on the methodological point beneath the finding: most research on families asks only one person, and response-surface methods are quietly showing how much that distorts the picture.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); self-report on both sides; single-country sample; the cross-age comparison is between-groups, not longitudinal.

studies.title: Gay and bisexual women veterans gain more from emotion-skills therapy after military sexual trauma
studies.ns_score_reason: overturns an assumption that a marginalized subgroup will respond worse to standard therapy; secondary analysis with only 42 sexual minority participants.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A secondary analysis of a randomized trial comparing Skills Training in Affective and Interpersonal Regulation (STAIR) with present-centered therapy in 161 women veterans who had experienced military sexual trauma, of whom 42 were sexual minority women. Both groups improved on PTSD symptoms, and both did better in STAIR — but sexual minority women improved *more* than heterosexual women on emotion regulation, post-traumatic maladaptive beliefs and depression, despite starting at comparable symptom levels. Therapeutic alliance and satisfaction were high and did not differ by sexual orientation.
studies.why_it_matters: The default assumption in trauma services is that minority-stress burden blunts treatment response and that bespoke programs are needed; here a standard emotion-regulation therapy worked at least as well, and on some measures better.
studies.pitch_angle: A group widely assumed to need tailored care did better on the off-the-shelf treatment. Open on what STAIR actually involves — learning to name and modulate feelings before touching the trauma memory itself. Call Marylene Cloitre (NYU) or Leslie Morland (VA San Diego). Be careful: this is a subgroup analysis, not a trial designed to answer this question.
studies.wider_angle: A longer piece for a health-policy or veterans-focused outlet on how sexual minority women are counted (or not) in military health research, and why so few trials are powered to say anything about them.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of an existing trial, not pre-specified; small subgroup (n=42); self-reported outcomes; predominantly White US veteran sample.

studies.title: Brain scans link punishment sensitivity to a surprising pattern of prefrontal wiring
studies.ns_score_reason: a decent-sized imaging sample (N=357) combining structure, connectivity and mediation; the key statistical result is a suppression effect, which is hard to explain in 600 words.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In 357 healthy university students, researchers combined questionnaires, voxel-based morphometry and resting-state functional connectivity. People more sensitive to punishment were worse at cognitive reappraisal — yet they had *more* gray matter in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a region central to emotion regulation, and stronger connectivity between that region and the right precuneus. Mediation analysis found this connectivity acted as a statistical suppressor, with direct and indirect effects pushing in opposite directions.
studies.why_it_matters: It complicates the tidy story that more prefrontal control hardware means better emotional control; here the same circuit that supports reappraisal appears to be enlarged in people who use reappraisal less well, hinting at compensation or overengagement of self-referential processing.
studies.pitch_angle: People who are highly attuned to criticism and punishment have more, not less, tissue in the brain's emotion-control region — and are still worse at reframing. Open on the everyday version: the colleague who replays every negative comment. Call Pan Feng or Tingyong Feng (Southwest University) and ask directly whether this is compensation or a rumination circuit in disguise.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-and-mind feature for a neuroscience-literate outlet on suppression effects in mediation analysis — the statistical phenomenon that makes a brain measure look like it's doing two opposite jobs at once, and how often it gets misread as a mechanism.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and correlational; healthy student sample only; emotion regulation and punishment sensitivity both self-reported questionnaires; no task-based validation of reappraisal ability.

studies.title: Bottling up feelings — not spirituality — predicts problematic porn use
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean null that separates spirituality from religiosity in a well-studied debate; small cross-sectional online sample.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A general-population online survey of 121 adults (mean age 27, 53.7% male) measured pornography use, problematic use, psychological distress, emotion regulation, moral disapproval, self-esteem and spirituality. Male gender, weekly use frequency, psychological distress and expressive suppression together explained 38.2% of the variance in problematic use. Spirituality, self-esteem and age showed no relationship at all — despite religiosity being one of the best-established predictors in this literature.
studies.why_it_matters: Much of what gets labeled "porn addiction" reflects moral conflict rather than loss of control; this suggests that conflict is specifically religious rather than broadly spiritual, and points at emotional suppression as a distinct behavioral pathway.
studies.pitch_angle: Spiritual but not religious people show no elevated distress about their porn use — the moral-incongruence effect appears to be religion-specific. Pair that with the finding that habitual emotion suppressors report more problems. Call Halley Pontes (Birkbeck), who works on behavioral addiction diagnostics, and ask where the ICD's compulsive sexual behavior disorder sits in all this.
studies.wider_angle: A cultural feature for a general-interest magazine on how "porn addiction" became a diagnosis in the popular imagination, and the researchers arguing that for many people the distress is about values, not compulsion.
studies.caveats: Small N (121); cross-sectional and self-reported throughout; convenience online sample skewing young; no clinical assessment of compulsive sexual behavior.

studies.title: Tracking the eyes while making an argument changes whether people act on it
studies.ns_score_reason: an odd and memorable manipulation with two-week behavioral follow-up, but the moderation only survives when the two memory measures are combined.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: In an online experiment in Germany, 230 participants had their working memory measured (forward and backward digit span), then heard a persuasive audio message about eating more fruit and vegetables. Half simultaneously tracked a dot moving horizontally across the screen — a load intended to occupy working memory and block defensive counterarguing. Two weeks later, self-reported fruit and vegetable consumption differed by working memory profile: people with relatively high forward span benefited most from the eye-movement condition. Tested individually, neither span measure reached significance.
studies.why_it_matters: It adds evidence that resisting persuasion is an effortful, working-memory-hungry act of self-regulation — and that occupying that capacity changes real behavior weeks later, at least for some people.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the strangeness: following a moving dot with your eyes while listening to health advice made some people eat more vegetables a fortnight later. Open on the honest statistical wobble — the effect appears and disappears depending on how the memory measures are combined — and use it to discuss how we judge borderline findings. Call Arie Dijkstra (Groningen).
studies.wider_angle: A skeptical feature for a psychology or technology outlet on the wider family of "eye movements change your mind" claims, from EMDR to attention-hijacking interface design, and how much of it holds up.
studies.caveats: Outcome is self-reported diet, not measured intake; key interaction non-significant when the two working memory measures are tested separately; online sample; single-message exposure; effect sizes small (η² ≈ 0.05).

studies.title: Anxious attachment predicts which children with ADHD stay traumatized a year after an earthquake
studies.ns_score_reason: rare longitudinal disaster data in a high-risk group; modest N and self-report instruments.
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 124 children diagnosed with ADHD at 3 and 12 months after the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes, measuring attachment style, family functioning, depression, anxiety and PTSD symptoms. Depressive, state anxiety and PTSD symptoms fell over the year while trait anxiety stayed flat. Poor family functioning and insecure attachment — especially anxious attachment — robustly predicted who still had elevated symptoms at 12 months, with avoidant attachment uniquely tied to PTSD. Children on ADHD medication had lower symptom severity across all domains.
studies.why_it_matters: For a group already prone to emotion regulation difficulties, recovery from disaster looks less like a function of exposure and more like a function of relationships — which argues for family-centered rather than child-only post-disaster care.
studies.pitch_angle: Two children survive the same earthquake; a year later one has recovered and the other hasn't, and the best predictor is how the family functions. Open on the 12-month assessment in Adana. Call Serkan Gunes (Adana City Research and Training Hospital). The medication association is observational and should be framed carefully — children on treatment may differ in many ways.
studies.wider_angle: A disaster-response piece for a health or humanitarian outlet on the children who get missed in post-earthquake mental health screening because their symptoms are attributed to a pre-existing diagnosis.
studies.caveats: Small N (124); single center; observational (cannot establish causation), including for the medication finding; no comparison group of children without ADHD; questionnaire-based symptom measures.

studies.title: Unit support protects deployed fathers from parental burnout — until combat exposure gets severe
studies.ns_score_reason: a clear "protection has a ceiling" result on an under-studied outcome; small, single-context, cross-sectional.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: 105 Israeli military fathers deployed to combat zones completed questionnaires on exposure, emotion regulation strategies, unit and spousal support, and four dimensions of parental burnout. Habitual emotional suppression was associated with more exhaustion, more estrangement from their earlier parenting self, and more emotional distancing from their children. Unit support predicted lower burnout — but only at low and moderate exposure levels; at high exposure the protective association vanished. Marital satisfaction helped mainly among fathers who used cognitive reappraisal less.
studies.why_it_matters: Social support is usually treated as a general-purpose buffer; this suggests buffers saturate, and that the fathers who most need support are the ones for whom it stops working.
studies.pitch_angle: "Emotional distancing from your own child" is a measurable burnout dimension, and suppression — the coping style combat arguably demands — predicts it. Open on a father returning from deployment and finding he cannot re-enter the role. Call Ofir Ben-Yaakov (Ruppin Academic Center). Frame the moderation honestly as a limit on a buffer, not a causal claim.
studies.wider_angle: A features piece for a general-interest or military-affairs outlet on parental burnout as an emerging construct distinct from depression — what it looks like, who measures it, and why high-demand professions may be producing it at scale.
studies.caveats: Small N (105); cross-sectional (cannot establish causation); all self-reported; fathers only; Israeli military context may not generalize; moderation analyses with multiple outcomes raise multiple-comparison concerns.

studies.title: A systematic review maps what prayer, chanting and meditation do to the brain
studies.ns_score_reason: first synthesis to span traditions and practice types rather than just meditation; narrative synthesis of heterogeneous, mostly small imaging studies limits how firm the conclusions can be.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A PRISMA-registered systematic review searched Scopus, PubMed/MEDLINE and ProQuest to June 2026 and synthesized 105 neuroimaging and neurophysiological studies published 1998–2026, spanning Buddhist, Christian, Islamic, Hindu, Santo Daime, Spiritist and Sant Mat traditions, and practices from silent meditation to mediumistic trance. Distinct signatures emerged: meditation suppressed the default mode network and boosted prefrontal activity, prayer engaged social-cognition networks, chanting and recitation produced limbic deactivation with gamma and delta changes, and mystical states showed the most widely distributed profiles. Long-term practitioners showed structural differences.
studies.why_it_matters: It shifts the conversation from "does meditation change the brain" to the more interesting question of whether different contemplative practices are actually different interventions with different neural targets — and prayer, the most widely practiced of them all, barely features in secular neuroscience.
studies.pitch_angle: Meditation gets the research funding, but half the planet prays — and the brain does something quite different when it does. Open on the practice-specific signatures, particularly chanting's limbic deactivation. Call Waqar Husain (COMSATS) or Haitham Jahrami (Arabian Gulf University), and be frank about the quality ceiling: these are mostly small imaging studies with no meta-analysis possible.
studies.wider_angle: A longer cultural-science essay for a general-interest outlet on the secularization of contemplative practice — how mindfulness was extracted from Buddhism and commercialized, while the religious practices it came from went unstudied.
studies.caveats: Review rather than primary research; synthesis without meta-analysis because of heterogeneity; constituent studies largely small, cross-sectional and unblinded; self-selection of long-term practitioners confounds structural findings; an erratum has been published for this paper.

studies.title: A psychodynamic online program shifts a personality trait in 10 weeks
studies.ns_score_reason: first test of internet-delivered psychodynamic therapy against neuroticism, and the mechanism finding is intriguing, but it is an uncontrolled pilot of 30 people.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Thirty adults with mixed anxiety and depressive symptoms completed 10 weeks of therapist-supported internet-delivered affect phobia therapy — a psychodynamic approach centered on tolerating avoided emotions. Self-reported neuroticism on the IPIP-NEO 300 fell by a moderate amount (d = 0.64) and stayed down at six months, with improvements in depression, anxiety, quality of life and emotion regulation. Changes in how adaptive participants' defense mechanisms were strongly predicted change in neuroticism (β = .63).
studies.why_it_matters: Neuroticism is the single best trait predictor of future mental ill health, and the question of whether it can be deliberately moved is genuinely open; this is a first data point for a psychodynamic, online route — and no more than that.
studies.pitch_angle: Can you edit a personality trait from your laptop? Open on affect phobia therapy's central premise — that neuroticism is partly a fear of one's own feelings. Call Tomas Lindegaard or Gerhard Andersson (Linköping), who run one of the largest internet-therapy research groups in the world, and let them state plainly that this needs an RCT.
studies.wider_angle: A personality-science feature for a general-interest outlet on the growing evidence that traits are more malleable than the textbook five-factor model implies — and what that means for people told they are "just an anxious person."
studies.caveats: Small N (30); no control group; uncontrolled pilot so regression to the mean and expectancy cannot be ruled out; all outcomes self-reported; authors include the developer of the therapy approach (Frederick, Center for Courageous Living).

studies.title: A transdiagnostic therapy adapted into Urdu passes its first test in Pakistan
studies.ns_score_reason: genuinely first-of-its-kind cultural adaptation with large preliminary effects, but it is a feasibility pilot against a waitlist.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Fifty-one adults in Pakistan with diagnosed anxiety and/or depressive disorders were randomized to a 14-week Urdu-adapted Unified Protocol — an emotion-focused, transdiagnostic CBT designed to treat multiple disorders with one set of skills — or a waitlist. Retention was 82.4%, homework completion 79%, and satisfaction high. Preliminary clinical effects were large (anxiety g = 1.18; depression g = 1.15), and qualitative feedback emphasized new emotional awareness.
studies.why_it_matters: Transdiagnostic protocols are attractive for low-resource settings because one training covers many diagnoses; this shows the Unified Protocol survives translation into Urdu with high engagement, which is the usual failure point.
studies.pitch_angle: One therapy, many diagnoses — and the cultural adaptation work that decides whether it travels. Open on a participant describing emotional awareness as a new concept. Call Asma Nisa (NUST Islamabad). Be explicit that this is a feasibility trial: the large effect sizes come from a waitlist comparison and should not be read as efficacy.
studies.wider_angle: A global-health feature on the "adaptation versus fidelity" tension — how much of a Western manualized therapy can you change before it stops being the tested intervention, for a health-policy or development outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (51); waitlist control, which inflates apparent effects; single center; retrospectively registered; self-reported clinical outcomes; feasibility endpoints were the primary aim.

studies.title: Putting people in a bad mood reveals different brain networks in heavy internet users
studies.ns_score_reason: a smart design that tests the brain in the state that actually triggers the behavior, undercut by a very small sample and partly preliminary results.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Twenty people with problematic internet use and 20 matched controls had resting-state fMRI scans before and after a negative mood induction, with independent component analysis used to compare within-network connectivity. Mood induction worked in both groups, but the problematic-use group showed distinct shifts in four networks, including the default mode and dorsal attention networks; the prefrontal-parietal default mode and dorsal attention effects survived permutation testing, while the limbic and temporo-sensorimotor findings did not.
studies.why_it_matters: Most imaging of problematic internet use scans people at rest in a neutral state — but the behavior is triggered by feeling bad, so testing the brain under induced negative mood is arguably the right experiment; the result is a modest hint that the difference is state-dependent rather than fixed.
studies.pitch_angle: Scanning people while calm may have been the wrong approach all along — the differences show up when you make them feel bad first. Open on the mood induction itself, in the scanner. Call Seçil Tunalı Aslan (Yeditepe University). Keep the framing exploratory: 40 people, and half the effects didn't survive stricter testing.
studies.wider_angle: A methods piece for a neuroscience-focused outlet on the limits of resting-state fMRI in psychiatry, and the move toward "state-dependent" scanning that probes the brain in the condition where the symptom actually happens.
studies.caveats: Very small N (40); single center; cross-sectional group comparison (cannot establish causation); limbic and temporo-sensorimotor findings did not survive permutation testing and are described by the authors as preliminary; problematic internet use defined by self-report.

citation_table.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **Expressive suppression keeps turning up as the cost-bearing strategy.** The new batch links habitual suppression to problematic pornography use (PMID 42766058), to parental burnout and emotional distancing in deployed Israeli fathers (42671804), and to teenagers who perceive more conflict than their parents do (42753047). That extends the previous digest's cluster: mothers' suppression predicting toddler screen time (42447742), suppression as the downstream product of momentary attachment anxiety in depressed and anxious patients (41885910), and agreeable people suppressing tears at a friend's bad news (42537321).
- **Moment-to-moment state beats stable trait.** The suicidal ideation EMA study — risk rises when impulsivity exceeds a person's *own* average, with trait impulsivity showing nothing (42778027) — is the sharpest version yet of what the previous digest found in depressed adults' experience sampling (42660575), in the dynamic modeling of disclosure and suppression loops (41885910) and in the polyregulation data (41806361).
- **Reappraisal's awkward status persists.** The imaging study in which punishment-sensitive people have *more* right dlPFC gray matter yet reappraise worse (42722323), and the finding that marital satisfaction helps mainly the fathers who reappraise less (42671804), sit alongside last run's repeated reappraisal nulls (42660575, 42413746, 42447742).
- **Family relationships, not exposure history, predict outcomes.** Family functioning and anxious attachment predicting which children with ADHD were still symptomatic a year after the Türkiye earthquakes (41910948), and caregiver distress as the lever on violence against children (42754240), echo the previous digest's refugee finding that post-migration social stress — not trauma exposure — severed people from interpersonal regulation (42619365).

**Advances**
- **From measuring co-regulation to intervening on it.** The previous digest was dominated by observation — second-by-second validation coding in couples (42441643), home audio of mothers (41642821), infant–parent heart rate coupling (42269373). This batch delivers the trial versions: a randomized parenting program that halved physical violence against children by treating caregivers' own distress (42754240), and an Urdu-adapted Unified Protocol feasibility RCT (42768329).
- **Contemplative practice moves up the evidence ladder — and widens.** Last run had uncontrolled VR mindfulness in children (41484577) and HRV biofeedback imaging (42669395); this run has a six-month randomized Transcendental Meditation trial (42778032) plus the first synthesis to put prayer, chanting and trance alongside meditation (42670176).
- **"Just-in-time" intervention gets a target.** The previous digest's wider angle on goal-sensitive app interventions (42660575) now has a candidate trigger signal: within-person deviation in impulsivity (42778027).
- **State-dependent measurement.** Scanning problematic internet users before and after a negative mood induction (42773324) advances the methodological argument running through last run's lab-versus-life mismatch in functional neurological disorder (42704885).

**Counterpoints**
- **Self-report reasserts itself.** Almost every finding here rests on questionnaires — including violence rates (42754240) and Rome IV gut symptoms (42749162) — which is precisely what the previous digest's preregistered FND study warned about, where reported dysfunction vanished under laboratory measurement (42704885).
- **Expression alone is not enough.** The AI-narrative dismantling experiment found that personalized material without narrative structure made positive affect *worse* (42714089), complicating the previous digest's broadly positive picture of disclosure and social sharing (41885910).
- **Tailoring may be over-prescribed.** Sexual minority women veterans improved *more* than heterosexual women on a standard emotion-skills therapy (41411035), against the minority-stress expectation that marginalized groups respond less well to off-the-shelf treatment.

**New themes**
- **Intergroup and political emotion regulation**, with disgust rather than empathy as the operative channel (42723350) — no analogue in the previous digest.
- **Large language models as both tool and experimental manipulation** in emotion regulation research (42714089), and smartphone sensing as suicide risk infrastructure (42778027).
- **Global mental health delivery** as its own strand: lay-delivered parenting in a displacement setting (42754240), cultural adaptation in Pakistan (42768329).
- **Deliberate personality change** — neuroticism moving in 10 weeks of internet-delivered affect phobia therapy, mediated by defense maturity (42735080).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Several studies in this batch independently find that psychological buffers have ceilings, and that they fail exactly where need is greatest. Resilience in 9,035 Chinese adolescents strongly reduced the odds of sliding into somatic-emotional distress but did nothing to pull out anyone already in it (PMID 42749162); unit support protected deployed fathers from parental burnout at low and moderate combat exposure and stopped working at high exposure (42671804); meta-humanization softened partisan hostility most at *moderate* perceived threat to social cohesion (42723350); and AI-generated text helped only when both coherent and personalized, with the half-done version leaving people with worse positive affect (42714089).

**Why pitch this now:** Resilience training, peer support and wellbeing tools are being rolled out across schools, militaries and workplaces on the implicit assumption that more protection helps more when things are worse — and four independent designs this month say the opposite, which also reframes why a caregiver program that directly treated distress (42754240) achieved what generic buffering does not.

**Angle:** A feature on the dose–response problem in psychological protection — how prevention science quietly assumes linearity, what saturation and backfire effects look like in real data, and why the people the programs are marketed to help are often outside the range where they work. For readers who have sat through a resilience workshop or been handed a wellbeing app at work.

**Potential headlines:**
- Resilience training protects teenagers who are well and does nothing for those who aren't
- Every emotional buffer tested this month had a point where it stopped working
- The support systems built for the worst-affected people are the ones that fail them

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — Mind already runs the constituent studies as news; the saturation thread is the argument those items can't carry individually.
- **The Guardian science desk** — sustained coverage of school resilience curricula and workplace wellbeing evidence, and an audience primed for the "does this actually work" framing.
- **Undark** — strong fit for an evidence-versus-policy piece on programs procured at scale on thin dose–response assumptions.
- **BBC Future** — regularly runs long, mechanism-led psychology pieces and would take the counterintuitive ceiling effect as the organizing idea.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Emotion Regulation — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-28 | **Studies reviewed:** 17
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-09-28

---

### Study 1: Halving violence against children by treating the parents' own distress
**PMID:** 42754240 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

All headline numbers check out: N=479, IRR 0.48 for physical violence at T2, IRR 0.69 for psychological violence ("nearly a third"), improvements in distress, PTSS, emotion regulation and psychological flexibility, and the null on children's emotional/behavioural difficulties.

**Issue A. Pitch attributes the effect to one component of a package intervention** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "The intervention did not primarily teach discipline techniques — it taught distressed adults how to handle their own feelings, and violence against their children dropped by half."
- **Abstract says:** "Parenting for Resilience, a co-designed, non-specialist delivered intervention to simultaneously reduce violence against children and improve caregiver mental health"; positive parenting, "parenting knowledge and beliefs, engagement in children's early learning" also improved.
- **Problem:** The trial tested an integrated package — parenting skills *and* mental health content delivered together — and reports parenting-specific gains. No mediation analysis is reported, so the claim that the caregiver-emotion component is the active ingredient (repeated in the headline, "by treating the parents' own distress") is not supported by the abstract. The digest's own study description gets this right ("tackles caregiver mental health and parenting skills at the same time"), so the headline and pitch contradict the body.
- **Suggested fix:** "Unlike most parenting programmes, this one tackled caregivers' own mental health alongside parenting skills — and violence against their children roughly halved. Whether the mental health component is what did the work is an open question the trial wasn't designed to answer."

*NS fit 7/10:* defensible — large prospectively registered pragmatic RCT with pre-specified primary outcomes; the self-report limitation is already named in the fit rationale and caveats.

---

### Study 2: It's how impulsive you feel today, not how impulsive you are, that predicts suicidal thoughts
**PMID:** 42778027 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Unsupported comparison between state and trait emotion dysregulation** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Emotion dysregulation predicted ideation both as a trait and, more strongly, as a momentary state."
- **Abstract says:** "main effects of tonic emotion dysregulation and phasic emotion dysregulation emerged as risk factors for concurrent and prospective momentary suicidal ideation."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports both as main effects with no statement that the phasic effect was larger. "More strongly" is an unsupported ranking that reinforces the headline's state-over-trait framing beyond what is reported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Emotion dysregulation predicted ideation both as a trait and as a momentary state."

**Issue B. EMA sampling frequency not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Open on the mechanics of an EMA study — a phone buzzing six times a day for a month."
- **Abstract says:** "30-day ecological momentary assessment period" — no prompt frequency given.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only; "six times a day" is a specific methodological detail that would need checking in the full text before it appears in a pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "Open on the mechanics of an EMA study — a phone buzzing repeatedly through the day for a month [confirm prompt schedule from full text]."

**Issue C. NS fit score and "overturning" language** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — 30 days of intensive real-time data overturning a trait-based view of suicide risk"
- **Abstract says:** Community sample of 103, all self-report, observational EMA; a single two-way interaction with concurrent (not prospective) ideation, "No other 3-way or 2-way interactions emerged."
- **Problem:** A 7 resting on one self-selected, self-reported, observational sample of 103 — where the key interaction held only for concurrent ideation — is generous, and "overturning" overstates a single non-replicated finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — 30 days of intensive real-time data challenging a trait-based view of suicide risk; held back by a modest, self-selected sample and a result confined to concurrent ideation."

---

### Study 3: Feeling seen as human by political opponents softens partisan hostility — and disgust is the reason
**PMID:** 42723350 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=1,541 across five studies in the UK, US and Canada; mediators (anger, disgust, empathy), outcomes and the moderate-level threat moderation all match.

**Issue A. Causal headline and "why it matters" against a correlational design** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Feeling seen as human by political opponents softens partisan hostility — and disgust is the reason" / "this points instead at a more visceral emotion — moral disgust — as the thing that has to be downregulated before people will talk to each other."
- **Abstract says:** "meta-humanization reliably predicts more conciliatory intergroup attitudes, with disgust emerging as the primary affective pathway."
- **Problem:** "Softens", "is the reason" and "has to be downregulated before" assert causation and necessity from mediation on what the digest itself calls "largely cross-sectional and correlational" data. The headline contradicts the Caveats line.
- **Suggested fix:** "Believing political opponents see you as human goes with less partisan hostility — and disgust, not empathy, is the emotion that tracks it" / "…this points instead at a more visceral emotion — moral disgust — as the pathway most strongly associated with willingness to engage."

**Issue B. Direction of the disgust pathway stated more precisely than the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the dominant emotional pathway was reduced disgust, not increased empathy"
- **Abstract says:** "with disgust emerging as the primary affective pathway" — the abstract does not specify the sign of the meta-humanization→disgust path.
- **Problem:** "Reduced disgust" is a plausible reading but is not stated; flag as unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "the dominant emotional pathway ran through disgust rather than empathy [confirm direction of the path coefficient from full text]."

---

### Study 4: Resilience stops teenage distress starting — but won't get you out of it
**PMID:** 42749162 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=9,035, ages 10–17, two waves 12 months apart, four profiles (~60% / ~20% / ~12% / ~6%), 81% and 56% retention, and the emotion regulation / family support / interpersonal assistance dimensions all match the abstract.

**Issue A. A null result reported as a definitive absence of effect** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "once a teenager's body and mood are both affected, personal resilience does nothing to pull them out."
- **Abstract says:** "baseline resilience did not predict spontaneous recovery from mild or severe distress (all p > 0.05)"; "shows limited efficacy in reversing established symptoms."
- **Problem:** A non-significant association is not evidence that resilience "does nothing" — particularly in the smaller severe subgroup, where power to detect recovery predictors is lowest. The authors themselves hedge to "limited efficacy."
- **Suggested fix:** "once a teenager's body and mood are both affected, baseline resilience did not predict who recovered."

**Issue B. Measured trait resilience treated as "resilience training"** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "'Resilience training' is sold as a universal fix, but here it behaves like a preventive measure only"
- **Abstract says:** Resilience was measured at baseline with the "Resilience Scale for Children and Adolescents"; no intervention was delivered.
- **Problem:** The study measured an existing individual difference in an observational cohort. Nothing here tells you how a resilience *programme* behaves. The pitch angle rightly warns against implying prevention, but the "Why it matters" line makes exactly that leap.
- **Suggested fix:** "Resilience is widely treated as a universal buffer, but the trait as measured here tracked only who avoided distress — not who got out of it."

**Issue C. Causal verb in the headline** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Resilience stops teenage distress starting"
- **Abstract says:** "Higher baseline resilience significantly buffered against transitions to more severe profiles" (observational cohort, odds ratios).
- **Problem:** "Stops" is causal language for an observational finding; the digest's own pitch angle instructs writers to avoid this framing, so headline and angle conflict.
- **Suggested fix:** "High resilience tracks with teenagers avoiding distress — but not with getting out of it."

---

### Study 5: Transcendental meditation cuts workplace stress in a six-month randomized trial
**PMID:** 42778032 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

n=65/n=64, Australian university staff, baseline/3/6 months, adjusted mean difference −2.25, Hedges' g = −0.52, and the secondary improvements are all accurate. Open-label design and absence of an active comparator are correctly flagged.

**Issue A. Dose-response finding restated as an attribution of the effect** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Exploratory analysis found the twice-daily practitioners accounted for most of the gains."
- **Abstract says:** "Exploratory analysis showed that twice-daily practice was significantly associated with improvements in perceived stress, well-being, HRQoL, symptoms of depression and burnout (p < .05)."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports an association between twice-daily practice and improvement; it does not decompose the overall treatment effect or say this subgroup "accounted for most" of it. The rewrite implies an attribution analysis that isn't reported.
- **Suggested fix:** "An exploratory analysis found that twice-daily practice was associated with improvements in stress, wellbeing, quality of life, depression and burnout."

**Issue B. "Primary outcomes" pluralised** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "all primary outcomes self-reported"
- **Abstract says:** "Symptoms of perceived stress (primary outcome)" — singular.
- **Problem:** Small imprecision; the trial had one primary outcome, with the rest secondary.
- **Suggested fix:** "primary outcome (perceived stress) and all secondary outcomes self-reported."

---

### Study 6: AI-written stories only calm you down if they are both coherent and about you
**PMID:** 42714089 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=87, three conditions, the Complete Condition as the only beneficial one, and the Self-Referential-Only backfire on positive affect all match.

**Issue A. Pitch reframes a reading study as a test of journaling** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Journaling advice, tested to destruction — and a warning about the half-done version."
- **Abstract says:** "AI text generation technology was employed to manipulate these components… Participants completed pre- and post-exposure assessments of state anxiety and affect."
- **Problem:** Participants *read* AI-generated text; nobody wrote anything. Expressive writing/journaling involves a different process (self-generated construction of narrative), so a pitch built on "journaling advice tested" rests on a result the study didn't produce. The "Why it matters" line ("'Writing it out' is one of the most commonly recommended emotion regulation tools") has the same problem.
- **Suggested fix:** "The ingredients of narrative-based emotion regulation, pulled apart — and a warning about the half-done version. Note the manipulation was reading AI-generated text, not writing, so this is adjacent to journaling research rather than a direct test of it."

**Issue B. "First experiment" overstates the abstract's own claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this is the first experiment to separate its ingredients"
- **Abstract says:** "its active components have rarely been isolated experimentally"; the authors describe the result as "initial experimental evidence."
- **Problem:** "Rarely" is not "never"; the authors don't claim priority.
- **Suggested fix:** "this is one of the first experiments to separate its ingredients."

**Issue C. Sample characteristics not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "findings from a Chinese student-age sample."
- **Abstract says:** No participant demographics beyond N=87; the only China link is the authors' affiliation (Jiangsu Normal University).
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only — the sample nationality and age band need confirming from the full text before appearing in Caveats.
- **Suggested fix:** "single-site sample [confirm nationality and age profile from full text]."

---

### Study 7: Teenagers' emotional habits track their own reading of the family, not their parents'
**PMID:** 42753047 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=1,875 dyads, adolescent mean age 13.06, 76.5% mothers, polynomial regression/response surface analysis, and the closeness→reappraisal / conflict→suppression split are all accurate.

**Issue A. "Consistently" firmer than the abstract's hedge** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "consistently across early, middle and late adolescence"
- **Abstract says:** "These associations were generally consistent across early, middle, and late adolescence."
- **Problem:** Dropping "generally" converts a hedged statement into an absolute one.
- **Suggested fix:** "generally consistent across early, middle and late adolescence."

**Issue B. Causal verb for cross-sectional associations** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "closeness and conflict shape different regulation strategies rather than being two ends of one scale"
- **Abstract says:** "closeness was more strongly linked to reappraisal, whereas conflict was more closely linked to suppression."
- **Problem:** "Shape" implies directional influence in data the digest itself notes is cross-sectional.
- **Suggested fix:** "closeness and conflict are linked to different regulation strategies rather than being two ends of one scale."

---

### Study 8: Gay and bisexual women veterans gain more from emotion-skills therapy after military sexual trauma
**PMID:** 41411035 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=161 with 42 sexual minority women, STAIR vs PCT, comparable baseline symptoms, and greater SMW improvement on emotion regulation, maladaptive beliefs and depression (all p = .002) are accurate.

**Issue A. Headline ties the differential benefit specifically to STAIR** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Gay and bisexual women veterans gain more from emotion-skills therapy after military sexual trauma"
- **Abstract says:** "SMW started off with comparable symptoms to heterosexual women but improved more on emotion regulation…, maladaptive beliefs…, and depression symptoms… than heterosexual participants. Regardless of sexual orientation, participants had greater benefits in STAIR." Conclusion: "SMW veterans may particularly benefit from therapies that focus on emotion regulation… (e.g., STAIR, PCT)."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports the SMW advantage across the trial, not as a STAIR-specific interaction, and the authors explicitly name both STAIR *and* PCT in their conclusion. The headline promises a treatment-by-orientation effect the abstract doesn't report.
- **Suggested fix:** "Gay and bisexual women veterans improved more than heterosexual peers in trauma therapy after military sexual trauma."

**Issue B. Alliance/satisfaction comparison probably misattributed** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Therapeutic alliance and satisfaction were high and did not differ by sexual orientation."
- **Abstract says:** "Therapeutic alliance and treatment satisfaction were high in both STAIR and PCT with no difference between groups."
- **Problem:** In context, "groups" most plausibly refers to the two treatment arms named in the same sentence, not to sexual orientation. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Therapeutic alliance and satisfaction were high in both STAIR and present-centered therapy, with no difference between the two [confirm whether orientation was also compared]."

---

### Study 9: Brain scans link punishment sensitivity to a surprising pattern of prefrontal wiring
**PMID:** 42722323 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=357 healthy university students, VBM plus resting-state connectivity, negative punishment-sensitivity/reappraisal correlation, positive dlPFC grey matter association, dlPFC–precuneus connectivity and the suppression effect are all reported accurately, including the "opposing directions of the direct and indirect effects" detail.

**Issue A. Measurement modality asserted in Caveats but not stated in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "emotion regulation and punishment sensitivity both self-reported questionnaires; no task-based validation of reappraisal ability."
- **Abstract says:** "the present study integrated behavioral measurements, voxel-based morphometry (VBM), resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC), and mediation analysis."
- **Problem:** "Behavioral measurements" is not specified as questionnaire-only; the abstract also refers to "cognitive reappraisal ability." The caveat may be correct but is unverifiable from abstract only, and it is doing work in the pitch ("ask directly whether this is compensation").
- **Suggested fix:** "punishment sensitivity and reappraisal assessed behaviourally rather than via a validated reappraisal task [confirm instruments from full text]."

---

### Study 10: Bottling up feelings — not spirituality — predicts problematic porn use
**PMID:** 42766058 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=121, mean age 27.3, 53.7% male, the four significant predictors, 38.2% of variance, and the nulls for spirituality, self-esteem and age all match.

**Issue A. Pitch claims a religion-vs-spirituality contrast the study didn't measure, and swaps the outcome variable** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Spiritual but not religious people show no elevated distress about their porn use — the moral-incongruence effect appears to be religion-specific."
- **Abstract says:** "spirituality, self-esteem, and age had no significant relationship with PPU… These findings provide initial evidence that, unlike religion, spiritual values are not incongruent with pornography use."
- **Problem:** Two problems. First, religiosity was not measured in this sample — the religion contrast comes from prior literature, so the study cannot show the effect is "religion-specific"; it can only show spirituality was null here. Second, the outcome was problematic pornography use (PPU), not "distress about porn use"; psychological distress was a separate predictor variable in the same model, so the swap is genuinely confusing.
- **Suggested fix:** "In this sample, spirituality showed no relationship with problematic pornography use — a contrast with the well-replicated religiosity finding, though religiosity wasn't measured here. Pair that with the finding that habitual emotion suppressors report more problems."

---

### Study 11: Tracking the eyes while making an argument changes whether people act on it
**PMID:** 42784902 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=230, Germany, online, forward/backward digit span, fruit-and-vegetable audio message, moving-dot condition, two-week self-reported consumption, higher forward span benefiting most, and non-significance when spans are tested separately are all accurate.

**Issue A. Headline wording misidentifies whose eyes and whose argument** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Tracking the eyes while making an argument changes whether people act on it"
- **Abstract says:** "participants (N = 230) were all exposed to an auditory persuasive message… Half of them were asked to follow with their eyes a neutral, horizontally regular moving stimulus."
- **Problem:** The headline reads as though the *persuader's* eye movements were tracked while arguing; in fact recipients moved their own eyes while *receiving* a message, and nothing was "tracked" — it was an induced eye-movement task.
- **Suggested fix:** "Moving your eyes while hearing an argument changes whether you act on it."

**Issue B. Effect size described as small** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "effect sizes small (η² ≈ 0.05)"
- **Abstract says:** "Combining both measures in one difference score revealed significant moderation (p < .001, η2 = 0.055)."
- **Problem:** By conventional benchmarks η² ≈ 0.055 sits at small-to-medium, not plainly "small"; the separately-tested interactions were the small ones (η² = 0.01–0.012).
- **Suggested fix:** "effect sizes modest (η² = 0.055 for the combined measure; η² ≈ 0.01 when spans are tested separately)."

---

### Study 12: Anxious attachment predicts which children with ADHD stay traumatized a year after an earthquake
**PMID:** 41910948 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=124, 3- and 12-month assessments after the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes, the symptom-trajectory pattern (trait anxiety stable), and the medication association are all accurate.

**Issue A. Headline assigns PTSD persistence to anxious attachment when the abstract assigns it uniquely to avoidant** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Anxious attachment predicts which children with ADHD stay traumatized a year after an earthquake"
- **Abstract says:** "Poor family functioning and insecure attachment styles, particularly anxious attachment, were robust predictors of elevated emotional symptoms at follow-up. Avoidant attachment was uniquely associated with PTSD symptoms but not with depression or anxiety."
- **Problem:** "Stay traumatized" reads as PTSD, and the abstract explicitly singles out *avoidant* attachment for PTSD. The body text gets this right; the headline reverses the attachment style attached to the trauma outcome.
- **Suggested fix:** "Attachment style predicts which children with ADHD still have elevated symptoms a year after an earthquake — with avoidant attachment specifically tied to PTSD."

**Issue B. "Best predictor" ranking not reported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the best predictor is how the family functions"
- **Abstract says:** "Poor family functioning and insecure attachment styles… were robust predictors of elevated emotional symptoms at follow-up."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports family functioning and insecure attachment together as robust predictors; it does not rank them.
- **Suggested fix:** "among the strongest predictors is how the family functions."

---

### Study 13: Unit support protects deployed fathers from parental burnout — until combat exposure gets severe
**PMID:** 42671804 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=105 Israeli military fathers, four burnout dimensions, the suppression associations, the exposure-level moderation and the reappraisal-moderated marital satisfaction finding all match.

**Issue A. Unit support described as predicting "burnout" generally** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Unit support predicted lower burnout — but only at low and moderate exposure levels"
- **Abstract says:** "higher unit support predicted lower emotional exhaustion and emotional distancing, but these protective effects were significant only at low and moderate war-related exposure levels."
- **Problem:** The association held for two of the four burnout dimensions, not the construct as a whole; the digest names all four dimensions earlier, so the generalisation is noticeable.
- **Suggested fix:** "Unit support predicted lower emotional exhaustion and emotional distancing — but only at low and moderate exposure levels."

**Issue B. Headline causal verb conflicts with the pitch's own instruction** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Unit support protects deployed fathers from parental burnout" / "Frame the moderation honestly as a limit on a buffer, not a causal claim."
- **Abstract says:** Cross-sectional self-report questionnaires analysed with hierarchical regressions; "predicted lower emotional exhaustion and emotional distancing."
- **Problem:** The headline asserts the causal claim the pitch angle explicitly tells the writer to avoid — an internal inconsistency an editor will notice.
- **Suggested fix:** "Unit support tracks with less parental burnout in deployed fathers — until combat exposure gets severe."

---

### Study 14: A systematic review maps what prayer, chanting and meditation do to the brain
**PMID:** 42670176 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

105 studies (1998–2026), databases and search cut-off, traditions, practice-specific signatures and structural findings in long-term practitioners are all accurately rendered, and the erratum is correctly flagged.

**Issue A. "PRISMA-registered" conflates a reporting guideline with registration** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A PRISMA-registered systematic review searched Scopus, PubMed/MEDLINE and ProQuest to June 2026"
- **Abstract says:** "Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered on the Open Science Framework, Scopus, PubMed/MEDLINE, and ProQuest (23 sub-databases) were searched from inception to June 30, 2026."
- **Problem:** PRISMA is a reporting standard; the protocol registration was on OSF. Small but the kind of thing a methods-literate reader will catch.
- **Suggested fix:** "A PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review, pre-registered on the Open Science Framework, searched Scopus, PubMed/MEDLINE and ProQuest to June 2026."

**Issue B. Claims about prayer's neglect in the literature are not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "prayer, the most widely practiced of them all, barely features in secular neuroscience" / "half the planet prays"
- **Abstract says:** The review synthesised prayer studies alongside meditation and others; it notes prior reviews were "limited to single practice types" but gives no comparative volume of prayer vs meditation research, and no prevalence figures.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. These are the load-bearing claims of the pitch hook, so they need sourcing before the pitch goes out — the review's own inclusion of prayer studies partly undercuts "barely features."
- **Suggested fix:** "prayer has attracted far less neuroscientific attention than meditation [verify from the review's study-count breakdown in the full text]."

---

### Study 15: A psychodynamic online program shifts a personality trait in 10 weeks
**PMID:** 42735080 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=30, 10 weeks of therapist-supported IPDT, IPIP-NEO 300 as the primary outcome, d = 0.64 maintained at 6 months, secondary improvements and the defence-mechanism predictor (β = .63) are all accurate, and the uncontrolled design is properly caveated.

**Issue A. Author described as the developer of the therapy** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "authors include the developer of the therapy approach (Frederick, Center for Courageous Living)."
- **Abstract says:** "Frederick RJ… Center for Courageous Living, Los Angeles, California, United States" — no statement of the author's role in developing affect phobia therapy, and no declared conflict of interest.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only, and potentially wrong: affect phobia therapy is generally credited to Leigh McCullough. The conflict-of-interest point may still stand in some form, but the specific attribution needs checking.
- **Suggested fix:** "authors include a clinician-author associated with affect phobia therapy (Frederick, Center for Courageous Living) — verify the nature of the affiliation and any undeclared interest."

**Issue B. Headline asserts change from an uncontrolled pilot** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "A psychodynamic online program shifts a personality trait in 10 weeks"
- **Abstract says:** "Results from an Uncontrolled Pilot Study"; "affect-focused IPDT shows promise… These results need to be replicated using a randomized controlled trial design."
- **Problem:** "Shifts" states an effect that a single-arm design with 30 participants cannot separate from regression to the mean or expectancy — which the digest's own caveats acknowledge.
- **Suggested fix:** "Neuroticism fell after a 10-week psychodynamic online programme — in an uncontrolled pilot of 30 people."

---

### Study 16: A transdiagnostic therapy adapted into Urdu passes its first test in Pakistan
**PMID:** 42768329 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N=51 (n=25/n=26), 14-week UA-UP vs waitlist, retention 82.4%, homework completion 79%, high CSQ-8 satisfaction, anxiety g = 1.18 and depression g = 1.15, and the qualitative emotional-awareness theme all match the abstract. Framing is consistent: the digest repeatedly labels this a feasibility pilot, warns explicitly against reading the effect sizes as efficacy, and flags the waitlist control and retrospective registration in Caveats. The 4/10 fit score is appropriately conservative.

---

### Study 17: Putting people in a bad mood reveals different brain networks in heavy internet users
**PMID:** 42773324 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

20 vs 20 matched participants, pre/post mood-induction resting-state fMRI, independent component analysis, successful mood induction in both groups, and four affected networks are all accurate.

**Issue A. "Did not survive permutation testing" is firmer than the abstract's wording** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the prefrontal-parietal default mode and dorsal attention effects survived permutation testing, while the limbic and temporo-sensorimotor findings did not."
- **Abstract says:** "The prefrontal-parietal Default Mode and Dorsal Attention effects were robust to non-parametric permutation testing, whereas the temporo-sensorimotor and limbic effects were preliminary."
- **Problem:** "Preliminary" is the authors' chosen hedge; "did not survive" asserts an explicit failed test that the abstract does not report. The Caveats line repeats this. The direction of the caution is right, so this is a wording fix rather than a substantive error.
- **Suggested fix:** "the prefrontal-parietal default mode and dorsal attention effects were robust to permutation testing, while the limbic and temporo-sensorimotor findings are described by the authors as preliminary."
